questions.q: What is the “forget it” test for a sentence in a lecture?
choices: Ask whether the rest of the lecture would still make sense if you forgot it.
Ask whether you could forget the sentence and look it up again later.
Ask whether the professor has forgotten to explain the sentence clearly.
Ask whether the sentence is one you already forgot from NICU Tutor.
questions.explain: If everything after it still makes sense, it's a detail. If the lecture falls apart without it, it's load-bearing — a big idea.

questions.q: “Most of the air, about 78%, is nitrogen; your body breathes it in and right back out, like a passenger who never gets off the bus.” Which is the big idea in that sentence?
choices: Most of the air is nitrogen, and the body doesn't use it.
Nitrogen makes up exactly 78 percent of the air we breathe.
Air behaves like a bus, carrying passengers in and out.
The body breathes nitrogen out slightly faster than in.
questions.explain: The 78% is a supporting number and the bus is a supporting picture. The idea is what they support: most of the air is nitrogen and the body ignores it.

questions.q: Where do big ideas most often hide in a lecture?
choices: In headings, in the first and last sentences of a section, and in things said more than once.
In the tables of numbers, in the dates of discoveries, and in the names of scientists.
In the jokes, in the pictures, and in the links at the end of the lecture.
In the quiz questions, in the homework, and in the flashback boxes only.
questions.explain: Professors state the idea, explain it, and state it again — so headings, section edges, and repeats are where to look. Tables and dates are usually details.

questions.q: In a 2006 experiment, some students reread a passage and others closed it and wrote down what they remembered. When everyone was quizzed a week later…
choices: the students who tested themselves remembered much more than the rereaders.
the students who reread remembered much more, because they saw it more often.
both groups remembered about the same, because they spent equal time.
neither group remembered much, because a week is too long to wait.
questions.explain: About 60% versus about 40%. Pulling an idea out of your own head (retrieval practice) builds the path; rereading only puts the words in front of your eyes.

questions.q: What did Leonardo da Vinci draw around 1511 that no one had drawn accurately before?
choices: A baby curled inside the womb, with its umbilical cord.
A premature baby inside the first incubator machine.
The four rooms of the heart with all of its valves.
A red blood cell as seen through a microscope lens.
questions.explain: His notebook page 'The Fetus in the Womb' came five hundred years before ultrasound. He drew it, asked a question about it, and wrote the idea in one line.

questions.q: Which of these numbers from this morning's Chemistry is worth keeping in your notes?
choices: Blood's normal pH: 7.35 to 7.45.
The pH of black coffee: about 5.
The year pH was invented: 1909.
The name of Sørensen's brewery: Carlsberg.
questions.explain: Keep the numbers a doctor would need at the bedside. Blood's pH window is one; the year and the brewery are details you can look up.

questions.q: How do this week's dashed “big idea” boxes work?
choices: Write your own idea on the notes sheet first, then click to check it against the professor's.
Read the professor's idea first, then copy it onto the notes sheet word for word.
Skip them, because the big ideas are now printed on the Class Notes sheet.
Click to reveal the idea, then write down every sentence in the section.
questions.explain: Write first, check second — that's retrieval practice. Next week the boxes only mark the spot; by Week 5 they're gone.

questions.q: From the isolette lesson, which of these is a DETAIL rather than a big idea?
choices: The humidity inside is often set to 70–85% for the tiniest babies.
Preemies can't keep themselves warm, so the isolette does it for them.
Getting cold makes a baby burn sugar and oxygen it needs for growing.
The machine adjusts its own heat by chasing a skin-probe reading.
questions.explain: Forget '70–85%' and the lesson still makes sense — it's a supporting number. Forget any of the other three and something important stops making sense.

questions.q: In chemistry, what makes something an acid?
choices: It lets go of loose hydrogen pieces, which is what tastes sour.
It contains extra oxygen atoms, which is what makes it fizz.
It is made mostly of carbon atoms, like everything living.
It has been heated until its molecules move around faster.
questions.explain: An acid drops off loose hydrogens (H⁺) like a bus dropping passengers. Those loose hydrogens are what your tongue tastes as sour — and what warps proteins if there are too many in the blood.

questions.q: On the pH scale, which number is neutral — neither acid nor base?
questions.explain: 7 is neutral, like pure water. Below 7 is acid; above 7 is base. Blood sits just above neutral, at 7.35–7.45.

questions.q: Vinegar is about pH 3 and milk is about pH 6. Roughly how many times more acidic is the vinegar?
choices: About 1,000 times, because each pH step is ten times.
About 3 times, one for each step down the scale.
About 30 times, ten for the first step and ten more.
About 100 times, because pH steps double each time.
questions.explain: Three steps down, and each step multiplies by ten: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000. That's why a ruler from 0 to 14 can cover everything from bleach to stomach acid.

questions.q: What is the normal pH range of blood?
questions.explain: 7.35 to 7.45 — a window one-tenth of a step wide. Proteins are shaped to work right there, and they warp if the blood drifts.

questions.q: What does carbon dioxide turn into when it dissolves in blood?
choices: Carbonic acid, which lowers the blood's pH.
Bicarbonate, which raises the blood's pH.
Lactic acid, which the muscles then burn.
Pure oxygen, which the hemoglobin carries.
questions.explain: CO₂ + water = carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), the same acid that makes soda water sharp. Every cell makes CO₂, so the lungs must keep blowing the acid away.

questions.q: A preemie's blood gas shows a pH of 7.20 and a CO₂ that is much too high. What is the most likely problem, and the fix?
choices: The lungs aren't clearing CO₂ — give more breathing help.
The kidneys are losing bicarbonate — give more fluids.
The cells are starving for oxygen — start antibiotics.
The baby is breathing too much — turn the ventilator down.
questions.explain: Low pH plus high CO₂ means carbonic acid is piling up because breathing isn't blowing it off. That's a breathing problem, so the fix is breathing help: more CPAP, ventilator breaths, or caffeine.

questions.q: What is bicarbonate's job in the blood?
choices: It soaks up loose hydrogen so acid can't do damage.
It carries oxygen from the lungs to every cell.
It makes the blood thicker so it clots when cut.
It turns sugar into energy inside the mitochondria.
questions.explain: Bicarbonate is the blood's sponge — a base that catches loose hydrogens. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, which is why it fizzes against vinegar.

questions.q: Where was the pH scale invented, and by whom?
choices: At a brewery in Denmark, by the chemist Søren Sørensen (1909).
At a hospital in France, by the doctor Louis Pasteur (1860).
At a university in England, by the chemist Joseph Priestley (1774).
At a soda factory in America, by the chemist Charles Alderton (1885).
questions.explain: Sørensen worked at the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory in Copenhagen. Brewers needed an exact number for acid, so he invented one — and hospitals have used it ever since.

questions.q: How many rooms does the heart have, and what are the two kinds?
choices: Four: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it out.
Two: one atrium for red blood and one ventricle for blue blood.
Four: two for oxygen, one for carbon dioxide, and one for plasma.
Three: one room for each pipe of the umbilical cord.
questions.explain: Upstairs atria receive; downstairs ventricles pump. Two of each, because the heart is really two pumps side by side.

questions.q: Where does the RIGHT side of the heart send the blood it pumps?
choices: To the lungs, to drop off CO₂ and pick up oxygen.
To the whole body, to deliver oxygen to every cell.
To the liver, where new blood is made.
To the left side of the heart, through the ductus.
questions.explain: Right heart → lungs → left heart → body → right heart. The right side runs the lung loop.

questions.q: A newborn's heart beats about 140 times a minute. About how many beats is that in a day?
choices: About 200,000
About 8,400
About 20,000
questions.explain: 140 × 60 = 8,400 an hour; 8,400 × 24 ≈ 200,000 a day. Twice what an adult heart does.

questions.q: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
choices: Red blood cells, using the hemoglobin packed inside them.
Plasma, the watery part that dissolves the oxygen.
White blood cells, which carry oxygen to fight germs.
Platelets, which carry oxygen to wounds to heal them.
questions.explain: Red cells are bags of hemoglobin — the no-nucleus cells from Week 1. Plasma carries sugar, salt, and bicarbonate; white cells defend; platelets plug leaks.

questions.q: About how much blood does a 1-kilogram preemie have in its whole body?
choices: About 80 mL — roughly a third of a cup.
About 800 mL — roughly a big soda bottle.
About 8 mL — roughly two teaspoons.
About 5 liters — the same as an adult.
questions.explain: About 80 mL for every kilogram. That's why every blood test is counted: 2 mL from an 80 mL baby is 1 part in 40.

questions.q: What is the ductus arteriosus?
choices: A fetal bypass pipe that lets blood skip the unused lungs; it should close after birth.
The vein in the umbilical cord that brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta.
The one-way door between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
A tube doctors place in a preemie's artery to measure blood pressure.
questions.explain: Before birth the lungs aren't breathing, so the ductus lets blood detour around them. At birth it should squeeze shut within a few days.

questions.q: Why is an open ductus (a PDA) a problem for a preemie?
choices: Blood leaks back into the lungs, flooding them, while the body gets less than its share.
Blood skips the lungs entirely, so the baby's oxygen level drops all the way down to zero.
The heart's valves stop closing properly, so the 'lub-dub' sound disappears entirely.
The umbilical cord stays attached to the placenta, so the baby cannot be moved or held.
questions.explain: Blood pumped toward the body sneaks back through the open pipe into the lungs. Breathing gets harder and the gut, kidneys, and brain get shortchanged.

questions.q: What did William Harvey show in 1628 — and how?
choices: That blood goes around in a loop, using arithmetic and the one-way valves in veins.
That blood is made in the liver, using a microscope and a drop of blood.
That the heart runs on electricity, using stickers on the chest of a patient.
That babies' hearts have a shortcut, using an ultrasound of a newborn.
questions.explain: He multiplied blood per beat by beats per hour and got far more than a body could make — so it had to circulate. Then he showed the valves with the finger trick from today's lab.

questions.q: What did Newton's prism show about white light?
choices: White light is all the colors mixed together, and glass can spread them apart.
White light is a single pure color that glass can tint into other colors.
White light is made by mixing red and blue, the only two true colors.
White light comes from the glass itself, which glows when sunlight hits it.
questions.explain: The prism bent each color by a slightly different amount, fanning the beam into a rainbow. White light was never one thing — it was all the colors travelling together.

questions.q: Why does a ripe tomato look red?
choices: It absorbs the other colors and bounces the red back to your eye.
It makes its own red light, the way a light bulb glows.
It absorbs red light and reflects everything else.
It bends white light like a prism until only red is left.
questions.explain: A thing's color is the light it refuses. The tomato soaks up blue, green, and the rest, and only the red comes back out.

questions.q: What lies just past red in the rainbow, where your eyes can't see?
choices: Infrared — longer waves, felt as warmth.
Ultraviolet — shorter waves, the sunburn part.
Violet — the last color the eye can see.
X-rays — the waves that pass through bone.
questions.explain: Infrared has even longer waves than red. It's invisible, but you feel it as heat — and the pulse oximeter uses it as its second color.

questions.q: Why does the pulse oximeter shine TWO colors through a baby's foot?
choices: Loaded and empty hemoglobin absorb red and infrared differently; comparing them gives the percentage.
One color measures the heart rate while the other measures the temperature of the baby's foot.
Two colors are brighter than one, so enough light can make it through a baby's thicker foot.
The red light warms the foot so that the infrared light can pass more easily through the skin.
questions.explain: Oxygen-loaded hemoglobin lets red through and absorbs infrared; empty hemoglobin does the opposite. The ratio of the two is the SpO₂ number.

questions.q: What was Takuo Aoyagi's key idea in the 1970s?
choices: Use only the pulsing part of the light signal, because only artery blood pulses.
Use a brighter red light, because babies' feet are thicker than adults' fingers.
Shine the light through the ear instead of the foot, because ears have no bone.
Measure the light with a camera instead of a detector, to see the color directly.
questions.explain: Skin, bone, and vein blood absorb light too, but they don't pulse. Keeping just the beat-by-beat wiggle isolates the fresh arterial blood — that's the 'pulse' in pulse oximeter.

questions.q: Why are bili lights blue?
choices: Bilirubin absorbs blue light best, and the absorbed light changes it into a form the body can flush out.
Blue light is the coolest color, so it doesn't overheat a baby lying under it for hours.
Blue light passes through the skin most easily and reaches the liver to switch it on.
Blue is the opposite of yellow, and opposite colors cancel each other out on the skin.
questions.explain: A yellow molecule absorbs blue. That energy twists bilirubin into a water-soluble shape that leaves in urine and bile — no liver enzyme needed.

questions.q: What did Sister Jean Ward's babies in the sunny courtyard show?
choices: Skin the sun reached turned less yellow, while skin under the diaper stayed yellow.
Babies in the sun gained weight faster than babies kept indoors.
Sunlight raised the babies' oxygen levels as measured by the pulse ox.
Fresh air stopped the babies' breathing pauses better than caffeine did.
questions.explain: A diaper-shaped patch of yellow was the clue. Light was clearing bilirubin through the skin — and Dr. Cremer built the first lamp from that observation, published in 1958.

questions.q: Why do babies under bili lights wear eye shields?
choices: As a precaution: a retina that's still growing doesn't need hours of bright blue light.
Because the blue light would otherwise turn the whites of their eyes a yellow color.
Because the bright light would wake them up and keep them from growing properly.
Because the shields reflect the light back onto the skin to speed up the cure.
questions.explain: The shields protect developing eyes from the brightness. (Ordinary NICU lighting was tested and does NOT cause ROP — oxygen does. The shields are about the bili lamp's intensity.)

questions.q: A feeding pump runs at 4 mL per hour for 24 hours. How much milk did the baby get?
choices: 96 mL
28 mL
48 mL
6 mL
questions.explain: Total = rate × time. 4 × 24 = 96 mL. 'Per hour' tells you to count hours.

questions.q: On a graph with the pump rate as height and hours along the bottom, the total amount given is…
choices: the area of the shape under the rate line.
the height of the rate line at the end of the day.
the length of the rate line from start to finish.
the steepness of the rate line at any moment.
questions.explain: A flat rate of 3 for 24 hours is a rectangle 3 tall and 24 wide — area 72, the total. Steepness was last week's question (how fast); area is this week's (how much).

questions.q: The pump runs at 2 mL/hr for 6 hours, then 4 mL/hr for 18 hours. What's the day's total?
choices: 84 mL
48 mL
144 mL
24 mL
questions.explain: Two rectangles: 2 × 6 = 12, plus 4 × 18 = 72. Add them: 84 mL.

questions.q: A baby gets a 15 mL feed every 3 hours. How much in a full day?
choices: 120 mL
45 mL
360 mL
15 mL
questions.explain: Every 3 hours is 8 feeds a day (24 ÷ 3). 15 × 8 = 120 mL.

questions.q: A 1-kilogram preemie takes 150 mL of milk in a day. In the doctors' units, that is…
choices: 150 mL/kg/day — about 'full feeds'
15 mL/kg/day — a trophic amount
1,500 mL/kg/day — far too much
150 mL per hour — a fast drip
questions.explain: Divide the day's total by the weight: 150 ÷ 1 = 150 mL/kg/day. Around 150–160 is 'full feeds' for a growing preemie.

questions.q: When the rate is a smooth curve instead of flat or stepped, how do you find the total?
choices: Slice time into thin strips, treat each as a skinny rectangle, and add them all up.
Use the highest rate anywhere on the curve and multiply it by the total time.
Use the rate at the very end of the curve and multiply it by the total time.
Measure how steep the curve is in the middle and multiply that by the height.
questions.explain: That's the slicing idea — Archimedes' polygons, Leibniz's stretched-S. Thin enough slices add up to exactly the area under the curve.

questions.q: Why do NICU nurses weigh diapers?
choices: Each extra gram is a milliliter of urine, so the diapers add up to the day's output total.
A heavier diaper means the baby is gaining weight, which counts toward growth.
The weight tells them how much milk the baby drank at the last feed.
Diapers are weighed to check that the right size was put on the baby.
questions.explain: Wet weight minus dry weight, in grams, equals milliliters of pee — because a milliliter of water weighs one gram. Output is a total that piles up, just like intake.

questions.q: How did Archimedes find the area of a circle, around 250 BC?
choices: He squeezed it between straight-sided shapes with more and more sides until the gap vanished.
He filled a circular bowl with water and weighed the water on a balance.
He cut a circle out of bronze and compared its weight to a square of bronze.
He measured around the edge of a circle with a rope and divided by three.
questions.explain: Hexagon, then 12, 24, 48, 96 sides, inside and outside the circle — the slicing idea done with polygons. It got him pi to better than three decimal places.

questions.q: Five heart rates: 120, 150, 130, 160, 140. What is the median?
questions.explain: Line them up first: 120, 130, 140, 150, 160. The middle one is 140. (The mean happens to be 140 too — that's not always so.)

questions.q: One baby in a group of nine weighs far more than the others. Why doesn't the median get dragged toward that baby the way the mean does?
choices: The median is just the middle position in line; how big the biggest is doesn't matter.
The median is only calculated after the biggest and the smallest babies are removed.
The median only counts the babies who weigh less than the group's average weight.
The median rounds every baby's weight to the nearest hundred grams before comparing.
questions.explain: Change the biggest baby from 1,600 g to 3,000 g and the mean jumps, but the fifth baby in line is still the fifth baby in line. The median only cares about order.

questions.q: A baby is at the 10th percentile for weight. What does that mean?
choices: About 10 out of every 100 babies her age weigh the same or less than she does.
She weighs 10 percent less than the average baby her age.
She is 10 percent of the way to her expected full-term weight.
She has gained 10 percent of her birth weight since she was born.
questions.explain: A percentile is a place in line out of 100. Tenth from the smallest end: about 10 in 100 are at or below her, about 90 are bigger.

questions.q: The 50th percentile is the same thing as…
choices: the median.
the mean.
the range.
the mode.
questions.explain: Fiftieth in a line of a hundred is the middle — the median. Half the group is below, half above.

questions.q: Ten babies are lined up by weight. Your baby is the 7th smallest. What percentile is that?
choices: The 70th
The 7th
The 30th
The 17th
questions.explain: Position ÷ group size × 100: 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7, so the 70th percentile. Seven of ten babies are at or below her.

questions.q: A baby born at 28 weeks weighs 800 grams — well below the 10th-percentile line for 28-week babies. Doctors would call her…
choices: small for gestational age, and look for a reason.
large for gestational age, and check her mother's sugar.
premature, but a perfectly typical weight for 28 weeks.
a normal full-term newborn who just needs feeding.
questions.explain: Below the 10th line for the week you were born is 'SGA' — a flag, not a diagnosis. The team looks for causes like a placenta that wasn't delivering well.

questions.q: A healthy full-term baby has been at the 5th percentile for weight at every checkup since birth. What does that tell you?
choices: She's a small, healthy baby who is following her own curve — that's fine.
She is falling off her curve and needs extra calories right away.
She has a hidden disease, because the 5th percentile is a failing score.
The chart must be wrong, because healthy babies are never that low.
questions.explain: A percentile is a place in line, not a grade. One baby in twenty is at or below the 5th by definition. What doctors watch for is a change — crossing curves downward.

questions.q: The Fenton preterm growth chart was built from…
choices: the birth weights of about four million babies from six countries.
the weights of about four hundred babies in one hospital in Canada.
a formula that predicts weight from a baby's length and head size.
ultrasound pictures of ten thousand babies still inside the womb.
questions.explain: Tanis Fenton's 2013 chart pooled about four million births. The honest catch: they were babies who were BORN early — often because something was wrong — so a different chart built from healthy pregnancies sits a little higher.

questions.q: When is the newborn heel-prick screen usually done?
choices: At 24 to 48 hours of age, after the baby has started feeding.
In the first minute of life, right after the Apgar score.
At the first checkup, about two weeks after going home.
On the baby's first birthday, when the blood is easier to draw.
questions.explain: Long enough for feeding to start and any pile-up to begin, but early enough to treat before harm. NICU babies get it repeated if TPN or transfusions could muddle the result.

questions.q: Why is the poke made on the SIDE of the heel?
choices: The side has plenty of blood and no bone right underneath it.
The side of the heel has no nerves, so the baby feels nothing.
The side is where the umbilical cord blood collects after birth.
The middle of the heel is too thick for the drops to come out.
questions.explain: Rich in blood, safely away from the heel bone. The poke is still real, so it's paired with sugar water, swaddling, or a parent's chest.

questions.q: What is PKU?
choices: A broken enzyme lets phenylalanine pile up and harm the brain; a special diet from the first weeks prevents it.
A missing hormone from the thyroid gland slows growth; a daily pill from the first weeks replaces it.
A wrong letter in the hemoglobin recipe bends red blood cells; early medicine keeps them from jamming.
A slow liver enzyme lets bilirubin pile up and turn the skin yellow; blue light clears it.
questions.explain: Gene → enzyme → job. In PKU the enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine doesn't work, so it piles up. The baby looks perfect at birth — which is why the screen exists.

questions.q: What is an enzyme?
choices: A protein whose job is a chemical task — snipping, gluing, or taking a molecule apart.
A kind of sugar that the mitochondria burn with oxygen to make energy for the cell.
One of the four chemical letters that the DNA instruction book is written in.
A hormone that travels through the blood to give the body's organs their orders.
questions.explain: A tiny worker with one skill, built from a gene's recipe. Thousands of kinds: some burn sugar, some digest dinner, one clears bilirubin.

questions.q: How did Robert Guthrie's 1961 test spot PKU from a drop of blood?
choices: Bacteria that need phenylalanine grew in a fat ring around blood spots with too much of it.
A chemical dye turned the blood spot bright yellow when phenylalanine was present.
A microscope showed the red blood cells bent into sickle shapes in a PKU baby.
The blood spot was fed to mice, and the mice with PKU blood stopped growing.
questions.explain: Guthrie was a bacteria scientist. His strain feasted only when phenylalanine was high — so a ring of growth meant PKU, days after birth and before any harm.

questions.q: PKU happens in only about 1 baby in 12,000. Why does every baby get tested anyway?
choices: It hides at birth, waiting causes permanent harm, early treatment works, and the test is cheap.
The test also measures the baby's blood type, which every hospital needs to know.
Doctors can't tell which babies are at risk, so testing everyone is a legal requirement.
The heel prick also gives the baby a small dose of the medicine that prevents PKU.
questions.explain: Screen everyone when all four line up: the disease hides, waiting is a disaster, early treatment works, and the test is cheap and safe. For PKU, they do.

questions.q: Which is the MOST common condition the heel-prick screen catches?
choices: Congenital hypothyroidism — too little thyroid hormone, fixed with a daily pill.
PKU — a broken enzyme, fixed with a special low-phenylalanine diet for life.
Cystic fibrosis — thick mucus in the lungs and gut, treated every single day.
Galactosemia — an enzyme that can't handle milk sugar, fixed by milk-free feeding.
questions.explain: About 1 in 3,000 babies, versus 1 in 12,000 for PKU. A growth-and-brain hormone runs short; one small pill a day replaces it.

questions.q: Which two newborn screens do NOT use blood?
choices: The hearing test and the pulse-oximeter heart test.
The Apgar score and the weight on the growth chart.
The PKU test and the thyroid test.
The brain ultrasound and the bilirubin light.
questions.explain: Tiny earphones and a sensor check hearing; a pulse ox on the right hand and a foot at 24 hours looks for the oxygen mismatch of a heart built with a missing pipe.

questions.q: What is attachment?
choices: The built-in bond that makes a baby seek closeness to a caregiver and explore from that safe base.
The habit a baby forms of loving whoever brings the milk, learned over the first year.
The wiring of a baby's brain at more than a million connections every second.
The reflex that makes a newborn grip a finger placed in its palm.
questions.explain: Bowlby argued it's a survival system as basic as hunger, not a side effect of being fed. Harlow's monkeys proved him right.

questions.q: In Harlow's experiment, baby monkeys could choose a wire mother with milk or a cloth mother with none. What did they do?
choices: Clung to the cloth mother most of the day and went to the wire one only to eat.
Clung to the wire mother most of the day, because that is where the food was.
Split their time equally between the two, feeding from one and sleeping on the other.
Ignored both mothers and huddled together with the other baby monkeys instead.
questions.explain: About 17 hours a day on the soft one — and they ran to it when frightened. Comfort beat food. (The experiments were also cruel, and wouldn't be allowed today.)

questions.q: In Ainsworth's strange situation, a baby called “secure” does what when the mother comes back?
choices: Goes to her, calms down within a minute, and returns to playing.
Ignores her and keeps playing as if she had never left the room.
Clings to her and cries for the rest of the session without settling.
Goes to the stranger instead, because the stranger stayed in the room.
questions.explain: Upset when she leaves, comforted fast when she returns, then back to the toys: the rope is strong and the baby knows it. About six in ten babies.

questions.q: In the still-face experiment, what did babies do when their mother's face went blank?
choices: Tried smiles and sounds to restart the game, then fussed and looked away — and recovered when she returned.
Fell asleep within a minute or two, because nothing interesting was happening in front of them any more.
Kept playing happily on their own, because babies that young don't really notice faces or expressions.
Cried immediately and could not be comforted for the rest of the day, even after the game resumed.
questions.explain: Babies expect serve-and-return and work hard to get it back. When the mother's face returns, so does the baby — within seconds.

questions.q: According to Ainsworth, what builds a secure attachment?
choices: A caregiver who responds to the baby's signals reliably — not perfectly, reliably.
A caregiver who never leaves the baby alone, even for a minute.
Feeding the baby on an exact schedule so it learns to trust the clock.
A caregiver who avoids responding too much, so the baby learns independence.
questions.explain: When she looked at the families, the difference wasn't in the babies; it was in how reliably someone came when the baby signaled.

questions.q: Why were parents kept OUT of premature-baby nurseries for much of the twentieth century?
choices: Doctors feared parents would carry in germs — a kind idea with a cost nobody had measured.
Doctors believed newborns could not tell one person from another until six months old.
Hospitals charged parents for each visit, and most families could not afford it.
Parents were thought to be too upset by the machines to be useful at the bedside.
questions.explain: From the 1940s to the 1970s, parents looked through glass a few times a week. Then Klaus and Kennell measured what early contact did, and the doors opened.

questions.q: What did the big 2021 study of immediate kangaroo care find?
choices: Starting skin-to-skin right after birth cut deaths of small babies by about a quarter.
Skin-to-skin made babies warmer but made no difference to how many survived.
Babies held skin-to-skin gained weight, but their mothers became more anxious.
Kangaroo care worked in rich countries but not in poorer hospitals.
questions.explain: More than 3,000 babies in five countries. Not waiting until the baby was 'stable' saved lives. Bowlby's rope is a treatment with a death rate attached.

questions.q: Why does bonding count as medicine in a NICU, not just niceness?
choices: It measurably steadies heart rate, breathing, and sleep, helps babies grow, and lowers parents' stress.
It lets nurses leave the bedside for longer, because a parent can watch the monitor for them instead.
It replaces the isolette for most babies, so hospitals can save money on machines and electricity.
It makes the baby cry much less, which keeps the unit quieter and calmer for all the other babies.
questions.explain: It's measurable — that's what makes it medicine. Which is why the reclining kangaroo chair is on the care plan and parents are on the team.

questions.q: About how many babies are born preterm each year, worldwide?
choices: About 13 million — roughly one baby in ten.
About 130,000 — roughly one baby in a thousand.
About 1.3 million — roughly one baby in a hundred.
About 130 million — nearly every baby born.
questions.explain: More than one in ten births. About 900,000 children a year die from it — the number-one cause of death in children under five.

questions.q: Why do sociologists compare places using rates like 'per 1,000' instead of plain counts?
choices: Groups are different sizes, so dividing by the group size makes them comparable.
Rates are always smaller numbers, so they are easier to write down.
Counting every baby is impossible, so rates are a guess that is close enough.
Rates hide the exact number of deaths, which is kinder to families.
questions.explain: A country with ten times the births will have ten times the deaths even if it's doing equally well. 'Per' means divide — the Calculus word — and dividing puts everyone on the same line.

questions.q: Where do more than six in ten of the world's preterm births happen?
choices: Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
North America and Western Europe.
East Asia and Australia.
South America and the Caribbean.
questions.explain: Two regions, most of the babies — and most of the deaths, because basic care is hardest to reach there.

questions.q: A baby born at 30 weeks in a rich country almost always survives. In the poorest countries about half of such babies die. What is the main reason?
choices: Lack of basic care — warmth, feeding help, and treatment for infections and breathing trouble.
Babies in poorer countries are born weaker, so the same care wouldn't help them.
Poorer countries have too many babies for the hospitals, so preemies are sent home.
The diseases in poorer countries are different and have no known treatment.
questions.explain: Not exotic things — the ordinary NICU Tutor things. The same baby, born in two places, gets two different lives. That's why kangaroo care and plastic wraps save so many.

questions.q: In the United States, which group of babies dies in the first year at more than twice the rate of white babies?
choices: Black babies
Babies born in cities
Babies of first-time mothers
Babies born in winter
questions.explain: About 10.9 per 1,000 versus about 4.5. Black babies are also born preterm far more often — about 15 in 100 versus 9 in 100.

questions.q: What is a 'maternity care desert'?
choices: A county with no hospital or clinic that delivers babies.
A hospital that has run out of incubators for its preemies.
A dry, hot region where more babies are born early.
A NICU that does not allow parents to visit their babies.
questions.explain: More than two million American women of childbearing age live in one. Regionalization only works if the Level III unit is reachable.

questions.q: What does 'social determinants of health' mean?
choices: The conditions of life — money, housing, food, stress, distance to care — that shape who gets sick.
The laws a country passes about which hospitals must accept which patients and at what price.
The genes a baby inherits from its two parents that decide how healthy it will grow up to be.
The social workers on a NICU team who help families with money, housing, and paperwork.
questions.explain: Circumstances, not biology. 'Your ZIP code predicts your health better than your genetic code' — and change the circumstances, and the numbers move.

questions.q: What did Dr. Virginia M. Alexander do in Philadelphia in 1931?
choices: Opened a clinic in her own house so poor Black families could give birth safely, then reported the gap.
Invented the first incubator for premature babies and displayed it at a fair to raise money for care.
Became the first Black woman in the United States to earn a medical degree from a university.
Founded the March of Dimes to raise money for premature and sick babies all across the country.
questions.explain: The Aspiranto Health Home: beds upstairs, pay what you can. Then Yale, public health, and reports the city couldn't ignore. Counting who isn't getting care is where change starts.

questions.q: Which of these sentences from Monday's Biology is a BIG IDEA rather than a detail?
choices: The heart is two pumps: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side sends it to the body.
A newborn's heart is about the size of a walnut, and an adult's is about the size of a fist.
William Harvey was the personal physician to King Charles I of England in the 1620s.
The umbilical cord has three vessels: two arteries carrying blood out and one vein bringing it back.
questions.explain: Use the 'forget it' test: forget the walnut, the king, or the count of cord vessels and the lecture still stands. Forget the two-pump idea and none of the rest makes sense.

questions.q: Blood came up in Chemistry, Biology, Physics, Genetics, and Calculus this week. Which statement is TRUE?
choices: Its pH must stay near 7.4, its red cells change color with oxygen, and a 1 kg preemie has only about 80 mL of it.
Its pH must stay near 5.5, its plasma carries the oxygen, and a 1 kg preemie has about 800 mL of it.
Its pH is set by the bones, its platelets carry the oxygen, and a 1 kg preemie has about 5 liters of it.
Its pH must stay near 7.4, its white cells carry the oxygen, and a 1 kg preemie has about 8 mL of it.
questions.explain: Chemistry: 7.35–7.45. Physics: oxygen-loaded hemoglobin is bright red and lets red light through. Biology: about 80 mL per kilogram — which is why every test's drops are counted.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.18 and a CO₂ far above normal. What's the story?
choices: Carbonic acid is piling up because the lungs aren't clearing CO₂ — give more breathing help.
The kidneys have lost all their bicarbonate — a kidney problem; give bicarbonate right away.
The baby is breathing far too much and blowing off acid — turn the ventilator settings down.
The cells are starving for oxygen and making lactic acid — start antibiotics at once.
questions.explain: Low pH plus high CO₂ points at the lungs. Low pH with NORMAL CO₂ would point at the cells. High pH with low CO₂ would mean over-breathing.

questions.q: Lemon juice is about pH 2 and black coffee about pH 5. How many times more acidic is the lemon juice?
choices: About 1,000 times
About 3 times
About 30 times
About 300 times
questions.explain: Three steps on Sørensen's ruler, ten times each: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.

questions.q: Where does the LEFT side of the heart pump blood?
choices: Out to the whole body — brain, gut, kidneys, fingertips.
To the lungs, to drop off carbon dioxide and pick up oxygen.
Back to the right side, through the ductus arteriosus.
To the placenta, through the vein in the umbilical cord.
questions.explain: Right heart → lungs → left heart → body → right heart. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pushes the farthest.

questions.q: A preemie has a PDA. What is happening?
choices: A fetal bypass pipe near the heart stayed open, so blood leaks back into the lungs and the body gets less.
A valve between the atria stayed shut, so blood can't get from the right heart to the lungs at all.
The umbilical vein never closed, so blood keeps flowing out through the belly button.
The heart's electrical spark is too slow, so the baby's heart rate keeps dropping.
questions.explain: Patent ductus arteriosus: 'patent' just means open. Before birth it let blood skip the unused lungs; after birth it's supposed to squeeze shut within days.

questions.q: Why does the pulse oximeter use both red and infrared light?
choices: Oxygen-loaded and empty hemoglobin absorb the two colors differently, so comparing them gives the percentage.
Red light measures the heart rate and infrared light measures how warm the foot is.
Two colors together are bright enough to shine all the way through a baby's foot.
Red light finds the arteries and infrared light finds the veins, and the machine adds them.
questions.explain: Loaded hemoglobin lets red through and absorbs infrared; empty hemoglobin does the reverse. The ratio is SpO₂ — measured on the pulsing part of the signal, Aoyagi's trick.

questions.q: What does blue light do to bilirubin?
choices: Bilirubin absorbs it, and the energy twists the molecule into a shape the body can flush out.
It bleaches the yellow color out of the skin so the bilirubin underneath can no longer be seen.
It warms the blood flowing under the skin so that the liver's slow enzyme starts working faster.
It breaks apart the red blood cells that make bilirubin, so that no more of it is produced.
questions.explain: A yellow molecule absorbs blue. That's why the lamp works right through the skin, and why more skin showing means a faster cure.

questions.q: A pump runs at 2.5 mL per hour for 8 hours. How much did the baby get?
choices: 20 mL
32 mL
2.5 mL
questions.explain: Total = rate × time: 2.5 × 8 = 20 mL. (2 × 8 = 16, plus half of 8 is 4.)

questions.q: On a graph with the pump rate as height and time along the bottom, the total delivered is…
choices: the area under the rate line.
the steepness of the rate line.
the height of the rate line at the end.
the number of hours along the bottom.
questions.explain: Height × width = rate × time = total. A staircase is several rectangles; a curve is many thin ones. Steepness was last week's question.

questions.q: Seven babies weigh 900, 1,300, 820, 950, 2,400, 880, and 1,000 grams. What is the median?
questions.explain: In order: 820, 880, 900, 950, 1,000, 1,300, 2,400. The fourth of seven is 950. The mean (about 1,179) got dragged up by the 2,400-gram baby; the median didn't.

questions.q: A baby was on the 50th percentile line a month ago and is on the 10th today. A doctor would say…
choices: she is falling off her curve — an alarm, even though today's weight is still 'normal.'
she is at a healthy weight, because the 10th percentile is still on the chart.
she has moved up in line, because 10 is a lower number than 50.
nothing, because a percentile is a grade and she hasn't failed yet.
questions.explain: A percentile is a place in line, not a grade. What matters is CHANGE: crossing curves downward means the growth line has gone flat. Read the line, not the dot.

questions.q: In PKU, what is broken and what happens because of it?
choices: The enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine, so phenylalanine piles up and harms the brain.
The thyroid gland, so a growth hormone runs short and the baby grows slowly.
The hemoglobin recipe, so red blood cells bend into sickle shapes and jam.
The liver's bilirubin enzyme, so the baby turns yellow in the first week.
questions.explain: Gene → enzyme → job. A broken worker means a pile-up. Caught by the heel prick at 1–2 days and prevented with a special diet.

questions.q: Why is every baby screened for diseases as rare as 1 in 12,000?
choices: Because they hide at birth, waiting causes harm, early treatment works, and the test is cheap and safe.
Because hospitals are required to collect a blood sample from every baby for its records.
Because most babies turn out to have at least one of the conditions on the card.
Because the heel prick also gives the baby its first vaccination against them.
questions.explain: Four things line up, and screening makes sense. A positive screen is a wide net — 'test again, properly, now' — not a diagnosis.

questions.q: What did Harlow's baby monkeys teach psychologists?
choices: Comfort matters more than food — they clung to the cloth mother and only visited the wire one to eat.
Food matters more than comfort — they stayed on the wire mother that held the milk bottle all day.
Baby monkeys can't tell a real mother from a pretend one made of cloth, so they clung to both.
Monkeys raised with two pretend mothers grow up healthier than monkeys raised with just one.
questions.explain: About 17 hours a day on the cloth mother, and straight to it when scared. Attachment isn't a side effect of being fed.

questions.q: In the still-face experiment, a mother goes blank for two minutes. What does this show about babies?
choices: They expect serve-and-return and work hard to restart it — then recover fast when the face returns.
They don't notice faces at all until about six months old, so nothing much happens for two minutes.
They prefer a calm, still face to a moving one, and settle down quickly once the mother stops.
They forget a face within a few seconds, so they treat their own mother as a complete stranger.
questions.explain: Smiles, sounds, pointing, then fussing and looking away — and back to normal in seconds when the game resumes. Every return is a brain connection.

questions.q: Country A has 200 preterm babies out of 2,000 births. Country B has 300 preterm babies out of 6,000 births. Which is TRUE?
choices: B has more preterm babies, but A has the higher preterm rate (10 per 100 versus 5 per 100).
A has more preterm babies and the higher rate, because 200 is more than 5 per 100.
B has both more preterm babies and the higher rate, because 300 is bigger than 200.
They have the same rate, because both countries are counted per thousand.
questions.explain: Counts and rates answer different questions. Divide by the group: A is 200 ÷ 2,000 = 10 per 100; B is 300 ÷ 6,000 = 5 per 100.

questions.q: In the world's poorest countries, about half of babies born at 32 weeks or earlier die. Why, mostly?
choices: They don't get basic care — warmth, feeding help, and treatment for infections and breathing trouble.
Babies there are born weaker than babies elsewhere, so the same care would not have saved them.
The diseases there are different from the ones that rich-country NICUs know how to treat well.
Their parents choose to care for them at home instead of in hospitals, for religious reasons.
questions.explain: The same baby, born in two places, gets two different lives — and change the conditions (kangaroo care, wraps, a clinic) and the numbers move. It isn't the babies.

questions.q: Flashback to Week 1 Physics: why is blood pressure measured in millimeters of mercury?
choices: The first pressure meters were literally a column of mercury: the push is how high it lifted the liquid.
Mercury is the silvery metal that the first blood-pressure cuffs were made from in the 1890s.
Blood is about as heavy as mercury, so the two liquids balance each other inside the meter.
Doctors chose mercury because it was the fastest planet, and blood is the fastest-moving fluid.
questions.explain: Torricelli's tube, 1643: the air holds up 760 mm of mercury. A blood pressure of 60 means the heart pushes hard enough to lift a 60 mm column.

questions.q: Flashback to Week 1 Statistics: a baby's Apgar score is 5 at one minute. What does that mean?
choices: The baby may need some help right now — rubbing, warming, perhaps a little oxygen.
The baby is doing well and needs only routine newborn care from the nurses.
The baby will have lifelong problems, because 5 out of 10 is a failing score.
The score was taken too early to mean anything and must be thrown out and redone.
questions.explain: 7–10 doing well; 4–6 may need help; 0–3 needs help now. And Apgar herself warned: it predicts the next few minutes, not a life.

questions.q: Flashback to Week 1 Genetics: what is a gene?
choices: One recipe in the DNA instruction book — the instructions for building one protein.
One of the 46 volumes of the instruction book, half from each parent.
One of the four chemical letters, A, T, C, or G, that DNA is written in.
A typo in the instruction book that changes how a protein is built.
questions.explain: About 20,000 recipes. This week you added one link: many of those proteins are enzymes, and a typo in an enzyme's recipe means a pile-up.

questions.q: Flashback: what does the isolette's skin probe do?
choices: It reports the baby's skin temperature so the isolette can warm or cool its air to hit the target.
It measures the baby's oxygen level by shining red and infrared light through the skin.
It counts the baby's heartbeats from the tiny electricity that leaks out to the skin.
It checks how much water is evaporating from the baby's thin skin and adjusts the humidity.
questions.explain: Servo control: the machine chases a target hundreds of times a day so the baby doesn't have to. NICU Tutor Lesson 1.

questions.q: Flashback: why is caffeine one of the most important medicines in a NICU?
choices: It keeps a preemie's immature breathing center awake, preventing apnea spells.
It speeds up a preemie's heart so that more blood reaches the growing brain.
It helps a preemie's liver clear bilirubin faster, so the skin turns less yellow.
It makes a preemie's blood a little more acidic so the lungs work harder.
questions.explain: The espresso molecule, in a measured daily dose. Steady breathing also keeps CO₂ — and carbonic acid — from piling up, as this week's Chemistry showed.

questions.q: Flashback: why can't a baby born at 26 weeks drink from a bottle?
choices: The suck-swallow-breathe rhythm is a brain skill wired at about 32 to 34 weeks; milk would go into the lungs.
Its mouth is far too small to fit around any bottle at that age, so it must be fed through a tube instead.
Its stomach can't digest milk of any kind until about 34 weeks, so it gets only sugar water in an IV.
Its teeth haven't come in yet, so it can't hold a bottle's nipple in place long enough to drink.
questions.explain: The throat is a railroad junction where food and air cross. Until the rhythm clicks in, milk goes in by tube — and the pump's mL per hour was this week's Calculus.
